Future radio interferometers can benefit from the efficiency of FFT-correlators, which replace computationally intensive methods with locally optimal algorithms, allowing for results to be reached in linear time. By substituting traditional correlators with these efficient algorithms, the limits of future interferometers are pushed, even beyond what is possible with traditional methods. Unfortunately, the increased efficiency comes at a cost of reduced sensitivity due to imperfect algorithms, a problem that hasn't been extensively studied for interferometry applications. Our research explores the cost of inefficiency across various algorithms, with results showing that the gain can be significant, up to 10% more sensitivity, even with minimal loss due to inefficiency, around 1-2%.

For several decades, the Markowitz mean-variance framework has been used to guide investment strategies, and recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to the application of generative models like conditional GANs for generating financial time series. However, traditional generative models ignore important information about relationship dynamics between assets, which limits their effectiveness for analyzing time-series data from interconnected financial markets. Building on recent advancements in graph neural networks, this paper introduces a new approach, RGCAN, which employs a fully self-attentive graph representation to represent the market data, thereby allowing the generation of realistic time-series data through a generated z-vector input, in accordance with the principles of good generative modeling. Empirical evidence demonstrates that RGCAN can generate time-series data accurately, maintain key statistical features of the market, and stabilize variance, in accordance with historical market data. Moreover, the model's ability to learn and simulate various market scenarios, including bull and bear markets, showcases its potential for stress testing and risk management. In addition, this paper introduces GenPareto, a new metric for evaluating the quality of generated time-series data, showcasing the superiority of RGCAN as a powerful generative model. Ultimately, RGCAN's versatility and adaptability make it a valuable tool for synthesizing time-series data across a range of financial applications beyond market time-series analysis.

We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element (POME) $A^{(n,0)}_{g\gamma}(z)$, a crucial component for the first two moments of the polarized structure functions for $n=n_{f}-1$, within Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). This derivation is a fundamental building block for reconstructing the polarized gluon distribution $\alpha_s\,xg(x,Q^2)$, especially after the recent resolution of the $g(x,Q^2)$ question. Specifically, it enables the reconstruction of the gluon distribution at any finite value of the quark mass, provided $n>1$, and this information is also required for the polarized gluon distribution $\alpha_s\,xg_\mathbb{R}(x,Q^2)$. In this study, the POME has been explicitly calculated in closed form up to the 3-loop order for $n=2$ and $n=3$.

A groundbreaking study successfully applied two innovative classification techniques to categorize Fermi-LAT blazar candidates into two distinct categories. These candidates had previously been divided into two groups, one comprising blazars and the other into non-blazars. We employed a combination of two classification methods, namely support vector machines and k-nearest neighbors, to classify the candidates using three distinct gamma-ray flux features derived from their emission characteristics. We compared the performance of these algorithms, using both binary and three-class classifications and evaluating their accuracy through various metrics, such as precision, recall, and the F-beta score. Our results demonstrated that the k-nearest neighbors algorithm excelled, achieving up to 90% accuracy in the two-class classification. Furthermore, we successfully identified a new high-peaked BL Lacertae object candidate, namely BL J1130$+$1677.

Social media is increasingly being used to express ourselves in visual and audio formats. 
Social network sites are increasingly being used to interact with others, 
while multimedia forms like personal branding and knowledge sharing are 
gaining popularity. 
Effective social network profiles are being cultivated to boost 
professional growth, while valuable knowledge is shared through 
educational videos and podcasts. 
We are launching Medimetrics, a project to analyze how 
multimedia content is used on social media, while exploring this 
field from a social perspective. 
This involves examining the impact of using multimedia, 
how users are influenced by it, and the impact on various social 
aspects such as professional development and knowledge exchange. 
Our approach is distinct from typical technical methods by 
focusing on social science, which is more suitable for tackling 
this impact. 
Our research will be conducted by interviewing users, 
analyzing their profiles, and exploring the impact of media on 
different social aspects.

In this paper, we propose a new approach to defining hypergraph operations using tensors and demonstrate the equivalence of three different formulations. This unified framework reveals the underlying connections among various hypergraph operations and facilitates the identification of relationships among their topological invariants. By leveraging this unified approach, we calculate fundamental properties of the tensor join and t-star operations on hypergraphs.

India has announced the INSIST, a space telescope, as one of its flagship missions for 2022. The mission, which has been selected by ISRO, is set to become India's first major space-based astronomical instrument combining the capabilities of spectroscopy and imaging. Insourced entirely within the country, it is expected to significantly expand our comprehension of the cosmos, from nearby to distant regions. The telescope, with an 80-cm aperture, is designed to achieve a high resolution of 10,000 in the visible and near-infrared range. Its comprehensive spectroscopic and imaging capabilities will enable a wide range of scientific investigations, spanning from the study of nearby stars and exoplanets to the analysis of distant galaxies and clusters. The telescope, specifically, is set to contribute to understanding supernovae, the detection of exoplanets, and a detailed examination of distant galaxy clusters. The INSIST mission is scheduled to commence in 2022 with its initial design, optical design, and development phases, aiming to launch in 2025.

In clinical trials, the widely used mixed model repeated measures (MMRM) approach typically assumes continuous time. However, when time is categorized, such as in clinical practice, this approach may lead to suboptimal treatment group comparisons due to loss of precision. To address this, our study evaluates various MMRM models with categorized time and introduces new models tailored to categorical time. By conducting simulations in a clinical trial setting, our analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of model correlation structure over the mixed effects structure. Consequently, our results indicate that categorical MMRM models, incorporating the interaction of categorical time and treatment in the mixed effects part and adopting categorical time correlation structures, provide reliable and precise treatment comparisons. These categorical MMRM models are readily available to implement.

A novel computational method called Action-based Transition Path Sampling (ATPS) has been developed to sample transition paths using discrete time steps, with substantial improvements in performance over Transition Path Sampling (TSPS). Action-based methods, such as TPS, rely on a continuous-path parameterization that suffers from computational limitations due to discretization. In contrast, ATPS circumvents this issue by shifting focus from path configurations to action values, allowing for more efficient sampling on a lower-dimensional grid. This approach enables increased efficiency in sampling discrete time steps, as action values can be readily obtained through dynamic simulation. Action-based weighting also reduces the number of grid points required, leading to improved performance in finding transition paths. Combining TPS and accelerated molecular dynamics methods can further decrease the required action range, allowing for even more efficient sampling. Convergence analysis demonstrates that ATPS achieves better performance compared to traditional TPS methods.

This study focuses on a parabolic variant of complex Monge-Ampere equations and utilizes a PDE-based method akin to Phong et al to derive and establish L-infinity and Holder estimates. Building upon this framework, we also develop L1 estimates and consequentially prove the continuity of the solution.

Building on automata theory and logic path semantics, we introduced polyregular functions, which grow at a polynomial rate. This class of functions naturally encompasses all topics previously mentioned, and crucially, it is stable under composition. To further explore this connection, we delved into the complexity of computing outputs generated by general weighted automata. We discovered that computing the result of a weighted automata computation in constant dimension is an FP-complete problem within the PSPACE range. Conversely, we found that computing the result in zero or sufficiently high dimension presents a straightforward and efficient solution. Additionally, we found that the complexity drops significantly in several cases. Furthermore, we explored the computational complexity of a related issue: determining the image of a linear transformation in combinatorial terms.

This concise note establishes a relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals when conditional measure flow components are involved in the integrands, with the 'correction' term requiring consideration of Lions-type measure derivatives. It is then demonstrated that Sato type stochastic differential equations, influenced by conditional measure flows, can be linearized into time-time Time Delayed Differential Equations (TDDEs).

This research aims to investigate various types of normal subgroups using a specific topology derived from hull-kernel-type topological spaces. We have made significant contributions by introducing a new class of normal subgroups known as primitive subgroups, examining topological properties such as separation, compactness, connectedness, and continuity in these spaces. Furthermore, our study paves the way for identifying spectral spaces among these subgroups.

This study addresses the challenge of generating high-quality SQL queries from natural language sentences across different domains, a critical task in text-to-SQL applications. The key obstacles in achieving this goal stem from the scarcity of suitable datasets and the necessity to accurately capture the semantic meaning of user queries as well as schema information relevant to the respective domain. To overcome these challenges, we propose a multi-task learning approach that leverages two established resources, namely Wikipedia and google's knowledge graph, for both text enrichment and domain adaptation. Specifically, we expand our model's capability to generate structured summaries from Schemas, while also synchronizing our goals of generating SQL queries and summarizing key entities from Schemas. Consequently, our proposed approach leads to significant improvements in SQL parsing accuracy on various datasets, including FinSQL, SchemaSQL, and Spider.

In complex multi-robot systems, accurately navigating while avoiding potential collisions between robots is a significant challenge due to the unpredictable movements of other agents. To address this, our method develops a decentralized, efficient approach that determines each robot's optimal trajectory to minimize collision risks, taking into account uncertain events affecting all robots simultaneously. By representing uncertainty as a set of probable scenarios, our approach calculates local risk at every movement interval using a non-negative, weighted probability distribution that is optimized in an online setting. This weighted distribution, constrained by a non-parametric robust model of probable scenarios, ensures a robust and efficient approach that can adapt to changing environments. Simulation results show the effectiveness of this approach in reducing collision risks and adapting to various uncertainty levels across a range of simultaneous probabilistic events.

Recent data on the dwarf spheroidal and blue compact dwarf galaxies around the M31 have highlighted a variety of metal-poor, low-mass, ultra-faint galaxies, some of which have very little gas and must have formed stars in the past. A key question remains about their origins: are they isolated galaxies or bound to M31. Our research focuses on the M31 galaxy groupies: Andromeda XXV and XXVI. The research utilized data from the 6.5m Magellan/Megamuse and the VLT/MUSE to investigate the galaxies' morphology, kinematics, and environments. Our findings reveal that Andromeda XXV has a velocity system of -87 km/s and is likely part of M31. Its mass within the 3.5' radius has a lower limit of 1.1 x 10^7 solar masses. The galaxies' interstellar medium shows a similar velocity to their stellar populations, suggesting the galaxies' dynamics are influenced by their surroundings. Our research indicates that M31 has likely absorbed and disrupted many small galaxies over the past 6.5 x 10^9 years.

In massive machine-type communications, utilizing grant-free access reduces latency and enhances efficiency by allowing multiple devices to share a common pool of resources, thereby generating minimal data traffic. Yet, this technique poses a challenge, as users can freely exploit the resources, making resource allocation crucial in ensuring that devices are assigned an adequate number of devices to ensure reliable transmission. Our proposed approach leverages a model known as a point process for device distribution and employs a model-free off-policy reinforcement learning method to train a controller that allocates devices to channels in real-time. By doing so, our scheme achieves stable channel load and meets reliability standards for a consistent device-per-channel ratio. Our simulation outcomes demonstrate that our method successfully achieves these goals without compromising on data reliability.

A comprehensive set of relationships was developed in the late 1950s to model the thermodynamics of moist air, employing alternative thermodynamic potentials and leveraging diverse variable sets. Each set of potential variables yields unique relationships, offering distinct advantages. We have gathered the complete set of equations in this review, aiming to fill an gap, as existing literature primarily addresses specific subsets, such as the alternative potential variables set proposed by Reichenbach and Koller in the 1980s.

We introduce algebraic objects, which generalise ordered semirings and monoids, and extend these to objects that include elements acting as negative identities. An exterior algebra analogue is proposed, which provides a negative analogue of standard exterior algebra semirings, and includes actions of elements that make it similar to the traditional form. Key examples are given, which illustrate how this concept works in different scenarios, and it is shown that certain examples have inherent functors that relate to standard exterior algebra examples.

Research in spoken dialogue systems has primarily relied on conventional top N ASR hypotheses based on frame-by-frame scoring, an approach established decades ago.  However, recent advancements in confusion networks, which condense the best N hypotheses into confusion networks, have demonstrated the potential to enhance system performance, as long as an effective scoring metric is applied.  Various scoring metrics, such as lattice-language model scoring and neural scoring, have been developed for confusion networks, each with their respective advantages and disadvantages.  In this work, we develop a novel learning algorithm, employing point-wise learning method, which enables frame-independent neural confusion network scoring models to be trained directly from a supervised dataset, thus circumventing conventional neural model training limitations.  Moreover, such point-wise learning algorithm allows the development of fully adaptive models without frame weighting.  Extensive experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of this point-wise learning algorithm relative to established alternatives, using data from the ISD2018 dialogue challenge.  Results indicate that the point-wise learning algorithm significantly outperforms conventional models, as evidenced by the improved word error rate of around 10% in comparison.

We examine the semistable coherent sheaves on a complex projective curve with a fixed rank and degree, and their enumerative invariants, calculated and expressed as the coefficients of a specific mathematical function, the modified multiple zeta function. This sheaf category is found to be equivalent to a moduli space of coherent sheaves, and its invariants can also be found topologically through a stable $S_1$-bundle over a complex curve of high genus. Furthermore, relations among invariants at different points and a connection to the multiple zeta function are discovered and formulated.

A critical factor in secret sharing schemes is the count of minimal qualified subsets, as knowing this can help determine the scheme's feasibility within specific domains, particularly in update and adaptive schemes, where the feasibility is directly linked to the number of subsets in infinity. A new method for constructing minimal qualified subsets in any probabilistic secret sharing scheme, leveraging a graph theory concept from Erdős, has been discovered, and it implies that any such scheme, irrespective of the security it offers, can have at most an exponential number of minimal qualified subsets.

To determine entanglement experimentally, we need to achieve optimal precision in measuring entanglement witness, which in our case involves a polarization state on two photons. Our proposal employs an approach that combines classical post-processing of measurement times or phases, which effectively enhances the precision of the entanglement witness in this quantum setup. This method proves to be equivalent to using polarized single-mode time bins, which also result in an optimal precision in this entanglement measurement. Furthermore, we've found that both techniques can be improved by utilizing times with multiple bins. Our research also reveals that the performance of the precision in these protocols depends on the relative phases between the times in the quantum setup. This work expands the concept of classical post-processing, which was previously applied in the field of optical coherent states, to include realizable non-local two-photon states.

Recent studies have achieved significant success in image-based continual learning. Pretrained models play a crucial role in many continual learning approaches, but they are often trained ad hoc and not specifically for this purpose. Our research demonstrates the potential of using a widely used frozen, pretrained model - ResNet50 - trained on ImageNet, to learn various datasets sequentially without any negative transfer, contradicting previous findings that suggested residual models are prone to catastrophic interference when fine-tuned. Our approach leverages the model's features in combination with regularization techniques, such as weight regularization and regularization entropy minimization, to achieve this result. Our experiments show that combining these methods surpasses image-based regularization and REPLAY methods across all evaluation metrics for six challenging datasets.

As social media platforms grow, so does the rapid spread of hate speech online, a phenomenon with severe consequences. In response, researchers have been working to create accurate social media hate speech classifiers. However, their research is hindered by the inherent subjectivity of hate speech, a concept that is difficult to define unequivocally. Consequently, researchers have been resorting to manually labeling social media posts, a process that leads to dubious results. This paper examines the limitations of current classifiers, discusses their potential drawbacks, and proposes an alternative approach. It involves training the classifiers using a combination of automated and human annotations, a strategy that proves to be more effective. In addition, we propose an AI-driven method for identifying diverse datasets for hate speech classification. In our experiments, the approach we present outperforms state-of-the-art hate speech classifiers.

We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the collective dynamics of these neurons. By applying continuous wavelet transforms, we enable the extension of these equations to networks with continuous distributions of in-degrees and out-degrees. These equations are then discretized and solved using a time integrator, allowing for the simulation and analysis of complex network behaviors. The results reveal the influence of degree distribution on the emergence of synchronized and desynchronized states in both inhibitory and excitatory networks.

Recent years have seen increasing interest in Automatic Program Repair (APR) with
numerous approaches being explored. One of the most promising directions involves
leveraging pre-trained neural language models (NMs) to generate repairs.
However, these APR methods are inherently limited by the output of NMs, which
often produce sub-optimal results. To address this, researchers have turned to
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) as a complementary technique.
In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of using GANs to enhance NM-based
APR. Our approach involves a discriminator trained to distinguish between
correct and incorrect program modifications, paired with a generator that learns
to predict the correct modifications. When applied to real-world datasets,
our method surpasses the performance of the underlying NMs in terms of both
success rate and quality of repairs achieved.

This study introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a complex interference channel, applicable to various forms of interference. Building on prior work in AWGN interference channels, which established a sufficient condition for optimal rates, we prove that this condition remains valid regardless of signal noise and signal to noise ratios in the more complex scenario. We prove that a set of lower bound rates, defined by a specific inequality involving mutual information and interference metrics, remains within the capacity region of the complex interference channel, irrespective of signal noise and signal to noise ratios. Notably, this inequality simplifies to previous known results in specific cases and provides more precise estimates for finite blocklengths.

Using $^3$He+Au collisions in 2019, we found that $2<$|$\eta_\mathrm{sys}$$<$5 and $| \phi_2^{\mathrm{even}}_2$| > in odd-numbered participants, contrary to previous findings in Pb-Pb collisions. Our results suggest that smaller nuclei like $^3$He exhibit stronger eccentric flows compared to larger ones like Pb. Furthermore, our EOS exploration reveals considerable variation in $v^2_2$ and $2$-particle correlation due to different anharmonic anisotropies from various EOS models. In anharmonic cases, flow coefficients aren't directly proportional to eccentricity but rather exhibit reduced values, especially noticeable in lighter collisions involving $^3$He. Additionally, using $2$-particle correlations and considering anharmonicities, we've identified optimal EOS parameters that maximize $2$-particle correlations in lighter collisions involving $^3$He. Our analysis also indicates that soft hadrons tend to exhibit more anharmonic behavior compared to hard jets in lighter collisions involving $^3$He, while showing harmonic behavior in larger collisions involving Pb. The rapid spread of the COVID-19 pandemic has affected the global population, with the emergence of the Delta variant causing a surge in cases in many countries. Effective management of COVID-19 relies heavily on early detection, enabling timely treatment and easing the burden on healthcare systems. Research indicates that point-of-care testing and clinical decision support systems are crucial tools. Machine learning techniques, particularly those applied to clinical data, show promise for detecting the disease early. Our study utilizes a novel machine learning approach to analyze the COVID-19 case load, utilizing the maximum mean discrepancy metric. Building upon an existing dataset, we analyze the distribution of features unique to COVID-positive patients. Initial detection is possible just three days after the first symptoms appear, highlighting the potential for early identification and effective medical response.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph-structured data. Recently, researchers have discovered that GNNs can successfully tackle various complex communication system challenges. However, GNNs face significant difficulties in handling channel coding tasks due to the substantial amount of prior information and system-level parameters involved in training, hindering their potential for implementation in practical wireless communication systems. This article addresses these challenges by presenting an innovative approach to applying GNNs to channel coding. It proposes efficient methods for simplifying complex GNN models and ensures their compatibility with hardware implementation. Furthermore, this article presents valuable insights and design guidelines for developing GNN-based channel decoders. Notably, experimental results indicate that GNNs can achieve performance comparable to conventional channel coding decoders.

The most prevalent cause of death in Brazil is the homicide, with Black people suffering the highest homicide mortality rate. The highest homicide incidence rates are also observed in the Western states of the country. Following the establishment of a national homicide database in 2004 by the Public Security Secretary's Office in Rio de Janeiro, data collection has been consistently implemented across the nation. Our study aims to investigate the spatial patterns of homicide mortality in Brazil from 2005 to 2019 using spatial statistics. The results indicate significant spatial autocorrelation in the data, with the Global Moran's I values ranging from 0.622 to 0.788 over the studied period. The Local Moran's I analysis reveals notable spatial autocorrelation in the low values observed from 2005 to 2019. The values of Global Moran's I show a slight decrease over the studied period, while the values of Local Moran's I highlight distinct patterns of spatial autocorrelation in the Northern and Southern regions, as well as in the Western states, respectively.

Optimizing smooth, strongly-convex functions is crucial in optimization problems and can be achieved using stochastic gradient descent with an appropriate step size that decreases exponentially. This method can reach the optimal solution in a finite amount of time in certain cases, but an exception occurs when the objective function includes multiple solutions. A reparametrization technique using a prior can help overcome this limitation, and we show that this reparametrized approach with stochastic gradient descent can efficiently converge to the minimum of the objective function in a Bayesian context, where the objective is a sum of a loss and a prior.

Axion and Axion-Like Particles emerge from a leading mechanism addressing the strong-CP issue in particle physics.  The alkali spin precession method has been extensively utilized to search for axions by detecting their characteristic frequency shift.  The alkali spin precession technique searches for axions by detecting changes in the spin precession frequency.  A novel approach presented here involves searching for axions by observing the shift in the spin precession frequency when an external magnetic field is varied.  This proposed technique complements existing alkali spin precession searches focused on measuring axion-induced frequency shifts in response to static magnetic fields.  This proposed method leverages high magnetic field resolution to effectively explore the axion mass-meson coupling space.  Axions can be effectively searched for by analyzing changes in spin precession frequency when varying an external magnetic field, utilizing high magnetic field resolution to unresolved mass-axion coupling space.

The occupation number over time is examined for Bosons interacting under various scenarios, either losing or gaining particles. This serves as the foundation for a universal, equilibrium-free method of information storage. As systems fail to reach equilibrium, both accelerating and decaying information processes can occur. The most effective storage method corresponds to the fastest information retention, ideally reaching the thermodynamic equilibrium state in a stable manner. This general framework can also explain the non-equilibrium dynamics of a Bosonic system influenced by external coherent radiation and demonstrate how its state can be stored.

We introduce DexGraspNet, a vast dataset comprised of over 300,000 images featuring diverse objects in various poses and sizes, collected using an advanced robotic setup with a dexterous gripper. Experiencing challenges in memory management due to its immense size, substantial breakthroughs in deep learning architectures have been leveraged to make the dataset accessible through a standard API. DexGraspNet boasts an extensive range of real-world data, encompassing a vast array of 10,715 objects in different configurations, which have been obtained through automated dexterous grasping. Utilizing this expansive dataset, we train and evaluate scalable end-to-end dexterous grasping policies that can transfer across unseen objects with remarkable success rates. Notably, DexGraspNet represents a substantial leap forward in terms of variety and scale in datasets designed for dexterous dexterous grasping tasks performed by robots.

A novel approach has been developed to create and optimize low-resolution MRI images that are resistant to respiratory motion, using a model-based framework that incorporates prior knowledge about motion patterns. This model-driven method divides stored input images into discrete sections, each representing a specific stage of respiratory motion, and relies on a parameterized domain transformation to generate high-resolution images from low-resolution images. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through MRI scans of human lungs at a relatively low spatial resolution, where a single input image can produce a series of distortion-free images across various respiratory phases. The associated source code is available for future use and improvement.

We propose Advanced Knowledge Distillation (AKD), a novel, efficient, high-quality compression framework based on knowledge distillation that surpasses current state-of-the-art performance, comprising (1) A Kernel Akd (AKD) operator that substantially minimizes computational complexity in the distillation process by representing the attention's similarity matrix through a low-dimensional kernel matrix, (2) Dual-level structure Akd, where the original model's structure informs the design of the low-dimensional kernel matrices, enabling low complexity while maintaining high quality, (3) Dual-level residual learning, where we introduce a dual-level mechanism that facilitates knowledge distillation at both coarse and fine levels, and (4) Dual-level entropy regularization that encourages students to generate diverse outputs at both coarse and fine levels. Our experiments reveal AKD's exceptional performance, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models across (1) visual recognition tasks (ImageNet, ShapeNet) and (2) visual understanding (ImageNet-VC) with significant improvements of over 20% in model size and 1% in top-1 accuracy.

Two submersion functions from the set of real numbers to the set of real numbers with two real parameters are defined within a specific open set. Equivalence in this context implies a smooth, positive function can map one set of parameters to another without altering the topological structure. This study determines the conditions under which two such functions are topologically equivalent, showing that under certain open set restrictions, equivalences of topological structures and regular foliations arise from bijective and smooth mappings. Furthermore, it demonstrates that for specific functions and foliations, any equivariant mapping is necessarily regular, provided each function has a consistent signature across its domains.

Ecosystems with plant cover arranged randomly, in uniform clusters, or with a regular spacing, have been studied since the 1930s, primarily along one dimension, despite a thorough understanding of the interactions between grazing, water and plant growth dynamics. Our research aims to gain insight into the interconnectedness of regular and random spatial patterns of vegetation in a desert environment by incorporating the effects of biological processes solely, using theoretical and numerical methods with reutilized data from a previous study. Specifically, our model demonstrates that the arrangement of oasis-like areas of vegetation, along with lower levels of vegetation in between, leads to enhanced overall plant growth and more resilient vegetation in face of arid conditions and heavy grazing, regardless of whether it's weak or intense. Our outcome suggests that the arrangement of vegetation in the Sonoran Desert Gypsum Plains significantly contributes to increased productivity and may offer a possible explanation for the observed resilience and patterns of the ecosystem.

A widely used dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch has limited applicability due to its focus solely on identifying prominent elements. To address this, we propose an improved CountSketch with enhanced accuracy. Additionally, we develop an extrapolated version of this modified method and compare it to a comparable reduced sketch technique employing explicit Oja's flow, which enables the computation of complete singular value decompositions for massive data matrices in a computationally efficient manner. Our approach involves a rigorous theoretical framework for both methods, including the derivation of robust theoretical error estimates for a complete set of singular vectors. Empirical results demonstrate the efficacy of our method on synthetic and real-world data.

We present a python-based auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo program specifically designed for simple diatomic and polyatomic molecules. After a thorough analysis of the different parts of QMC, we propose a modular and parallel architecture to boost computational performance. This innovative design results in minimal coding efforts to gain substantial speedups of a factor of 2-3, and even up to 15 for certain CPUs when dealing with certain molecule configurations. However, speed gains diminish as problems become more complex, with up to a factor of 5.5 for some molecule configurations. This new program offers users the ability to carry out full ab initio calculations on molecules within current hardware capabilities.

High-frequency trading, a high-technology strategy that uses computers to execute stock trades quickly, has been increasingly utilized by large financial institutions. As HFT continues to evolve, it presents an opportunity for further development in theory. In our research, we examined the impact of HFT from the perspective of theoretical constraints. We modeled the trading process as a game between multiple traders, each seeking to maximize their profits based on available information. In a standard market setting, traditional trading methods typically take a few seconds, allowing for real-time monitoring and adjustment. In contrast, H traders can submit orders as soon as market data is received, essentially eliminating the delay. In theory, if there are N traders with M available data points, profits can be calculated within N x M frames. However, if M is large, the delay can become a significant issue. In our analysis, the trader's profit at any point in time is determined by their current state and a series of past observations, leading to a difference equation. In this context, the difference equation can be approximated by a differential equation with time derivatives, allowing for a more accurate representation of the problem. In our theoretical framework, the optimal HFT strategy can be found by solving a system of linear equations, leading to a specific type of solution known as the "fast-slow" problem. In our analysis, the fast-slow problem arises from the interaction between the fast and slow time scales, leading to an interesting phenomenon where the system tends to settle into

We examine a first-price, second-degree information asymmetry auction model featuring $n$ competing buyers valuing $m$ (where $m\ge n$) separate, independent items. These items can be sold via package auctions or as individual items. All buyers provide identical valuations for each item following an i.i.d. exponential distribution. A mechanism design approach is employed to find optimal revenue-generating mechanisms and dominant strategy bidding functions in separate auctions: full package auctions and single-item auctions. Our study reveals that no uniform closed-form solution exists for optimal bidding functions in package auctions. However, a closed-form solution is found for optimal bidding functions in single-item auctions. A key finding is that a specific direct mechanism, which allocates items to high-bidding buyers and collects payments from them, is optimal, with payment rules being piecewise linear and non-increasing functions of buyers' bids. We demonstrate that weak monotonicity is not a necessary condition for incentive compatibility. A comparison of revenues generated by full package auctions and single-item auctions shows single-item auctions to be strictly more profitable. A case study with four buyers and three items is used to illustrate our findings.

To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've introduced an enhanced objective function that incorporates external knowledge through a new representation known as entity chains, which organize information about entities based on their properties and relationships. These entity chains guide the summary generation process, ensuring more precise outcomes, while our algorithm allows for efficient optimization. In our experiments, we've found that incorporating entity chains enhances the coherence and accuracy of generated summaries, surpassing other baseline summaries in outcomes from three different tasks.

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables, where these conditions are grounded in the differentiability of simpler functions with fewer variables and are, furthermore, less restrictive than existing well-known theories.

A recent study applied a realizability technique to establish the meaning of a quantum lambda calculus, which results in a multitude of acceptable typing rules, all conforming to operational constraints, thereby ensuring their consistency. Moreover, an alternative set of typing rules is presented, along with a corresponding proof of their validity within the calculus. In contrast to conventional techniques utilizing real positive numbers, these new rules incorporate Mackie's denormalized real numbers, offering significant advantages in terms of abstract manipulation and eliminating the necessity for circular definitions typically associated with quantum operations. Consequently, this approach effectively bridges the gap between computability theory and quantum physics, as well as continuous math and discrete math. Additionally, real numbers can be substituted with alternative denormalized real systems that adhere to the principles of idempotency, facilitating the translation of classical theorems regarding continuous lambda calculus to their quantum equivalents.

Analytical calculations have been performed for the quasiparticle excitation energies, delocalized composite fermions momentum distribution, and localized composite fermions spatial overlap integral, encompassing both Laughlin and composite fermions theories for systems with 2 or fewer extra electrons.

This paper focuses on thoroughly analyzing a particular type of mathematical model known as Stokes variational inequalities, which are typically used in glaciology to investigate the behavior of ice sheets. Under certain assumptions, it is demonstrated that this model has both a single, definitive solution and that the solution's behavior can be accurately predicted when the model's parameters are slightly changed. Furthermore, it is found that the model can be effectively reformulated as a coupled type of system of equations and inequalities. To achieve this reformulation, it is required that the model's parameters belong to a particular type of mathematical space. Under these conditions, the existence of the model's solution can be established. What is more, the single, definitive solution observed when the parameters are in a narrower range can also be applied to this reformulated model when the parameters are slightly expanded to a broader range.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. By incorporating ANNA v2, our model accurately simulated all anisotropic flow coefficients except for $v_3$ in central Au+Au collisions. A key discovery regarding $v_3$ in central Au+Au collisions revealed it to be nearly independent of centrality, contradicting model predictions. ANNA v2, however, successfully accounted for the dependence of $v_n$ on centrality, indicating that the anisotropic geometry is well-evolved into an elliptical shape, with minimal higher-order modes. Furthermore, our study showed that the energy loss of quarks in these collisions is consistent, as evidenced by the lack of variation in the ratio of d+Au to non-central Au+Au $v_3$ values when adjusted based on density.

Our proposed method effectively addresses the intricate challenges associated with coordinating a swarm of robots in dynamic environments, where multiple robots execute simultaneous maneuvers across different areas. This coordination challenge arises in various robotic applications, including aerial surveillance, aerial object transportation, and aerial imaging tasks. A key requirement for these systems is the ability to synchronize robot maneuvers in real-time, allowing for a transparent, coordinated interaction between the high-level decision-making system and the individual robots executing maneuvers. Existing communication protocols, designed for ground-based robots, are not suitable for aerial systems, mainly due to their reliance on GPS, which poses security risks through signal spoofing. Our transparent synchronization approach combines local time tracking and distance measurement to create a decentralized system that operates independently of the swarm members' locations. This approach was compared to traditional decentralized and centralized communication systems through simulations and real-world tests involving a drone swarm, showcasing its superiority in terms of transparency and overall performance.

Deep neural networks for semantic segmentation are typically pre-trained using
unsupervised image features, such as depth maps, but generating high-quality
unlabeled depth data is prove challenging. In an effort to circumvent this
issue, our research explores the feasibility of using depth estimation from
unlabeled videos to create highly detailed pre-training data for semantic
segmentation tasks. A novel self-supervised network called DSOSNet is proposed
that learns depth maps from videos solely through self-supervision, avoiding the
need for ground truth depth data. Furthermore, our experiments confirm that
using DSOS depth maps as a pre-training tool enhances semantic segmentation
results, demonstrating that DSOSNet effectively extracts meaningful visual
information, despite its depth maps differing from ground truth depth data,
which highlights the importance of accurately extracting and learning visual
information over accurate depth estimation itself. The code for our approach
has been made available at https://github.com/ChengqiDu/DSOSNet.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau for functional data is examined. A method for computing this measure is proposed and its asymptotic properties are used to develop a test of independence. The method is used to iteratively decompose Kendall's tau and functionally integrated versions of it into pairwise comparisons of individual subjects, functionally tested against constant values of zero. Both for ordinary and functional cases, the method leads to a cluster-based approach which reduces computational complexity as sample size increases, along with correction for estimated parameters via bootstrap resampling. Using synthetic data as well as real data examples collected from functional near-infrared imaging, we demonstrate the application and utility of this method.

The convergence of intelligent transportation systems and smart cities has paved the way for innovative applications, with advanced computing and connectivity enabling automated driving, intelligent speed management, and emergency vehicle prioritization. As edge intelligence systems are integrated into transportation infrastructure, there is a growing need for efficient and intelligent traffic signal optimization, real-time accident detection, and accurate passenger count predictions for urban transit. Our research focuses on developing novel machine learning algorithms tailored for edge devices, focusing on two key problems: enhancing edge networks and developing accurate accident prediction models. An EAS algorithm is developed to optimize resource allocation and prevent congestion, while a TSA algorithm leverages time-series data analysis and pattern matching for accident prediction. Our simulations demonstrate the superiority of our algorithms over traditional deep learning methods.

We explore the Euler characteristic and its generalized versions for topological spaces with singularities and issues in tangent bundles. This includes the topological Euler characteristic, Tu's local indices, and other related concepts. By examining various identities, we demonstrate the underlying connections between different theories, and examine how they apply in field theory.

Our analysis focuses on an adjusted predator-prey model incorporating a dual-species Allee effect, which usingqualitative theory methods, identifies conditions for coexistence and extinction that can be represented in a parameter plane. Furthermore, we explore how time delays affect this system's stability, developing both analytical and graphical insights into the interaction between critical delays and unstable limit cycles. This is complemented by numerical simulation results, which validate and illustrate these theoretical findings.

The Hirsch Conjecture was a theory claiming that a d-dimensional polytope with n faces cannot exceed a diameter of n - d. This assumption was contested by Santos, whose findings led to the conclusion that some linear programming methods cannot perform optimally within n - d iterations. This series of research was initiated by a novel algorithm, the facet pivot method, proposed in the first paper. This second paper verifies the efficacy of the facet pivot method, confirming it can solve linear programming problems within a maximum of m - d iterations, where m represents the number of facets of the polyhedron, and d represents its dimension.

We explore in an associative ring R with identity, the scarcity of k-torsion in the NK1GQ(R), which are Bass nil-groups for general and unitary quadratic groups. Our analysis also extends to a comparison between torsion in these groups and their corresponding general and unitary quadratic groups.

This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, off-shell computation for pp -> ttj events, particularly focusing on the dileptonic decay channel, with an approximation based on the narrow width assumption. Our goal is to quantify the magnitude of off-shell and non-resonant influences on the forms of various differential distributions that will be crucial for top quark mass determination through template fitting techniques in the future. The distributions examined include invariant masses of top systems and sub-components, as well as variables related to momentum and angular displacements, the magnitude of transverse momenta, missing transverse energy, events with low event yields, and the events with one or more b-jets.

The widespread adoption of facial recognition technology in security applications like smartphone unlocking, payment processing, and surveillance is hindered by its vulnerability to spoofing attacks. While current solutions rely on hardware or software to detect 3D mask attacks, a novel, hardware-free and hardware-resistant software solution has been proposed to detect both 2D and 3D mask attacks. The approach utilizes a smartphone camera to capture images, analyzing them through deep learning models trained on diverse, real-world image datasets. The projected soft-Riemannian gradient descent is applied to update the tangent space neural tangent kernel, boosting model performance on standard datasets like CelebA and WebFace. The results demonstrate the model's efficacy in real-world settings, boasting a 99.38% accuracy in identifying mask attacks, a 98.32% accuracy in clean image classification, and significantly outperforming the state-of-the-art by 1-2%. The project's code and models are publicly accessible on GitHub, with associated datasets available for download and further research.

In the realm of autonomous vehicle control, supervised learning has been widely applied due to its simplicity and reliability in delivering precise predictions. The fundamental challenge, however, arises from access to limited driving experience, making it difficult to accurately refine the initial model generated from log data using real-time performance feedback. To address this issue, we propose a new method that facilitates continuous vehicle improvement through real-world performance evaluation. Our approach is grounded in a novel theoretical framework that models the vehicle's behavior and its performance under diverse weather conditions and road surface variations. This framework is built upon a CarSim vehicle simulation environment that introduces realistic uncertainties into the vehicle's movement dynamics and environmental sensing. Using our proposed method, we demonstrate how a vehicle can adapt to unanticipated changes in its operating environment and achieve a substantial 20% reduction in tracking error compared to a standard supervised learning approach.

Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years, driven by parallel computing techniques that parallelize both loop-level and population-level operations. To further improve parallel processing, a new approach is proposed for evaluating function values in parallel evolutionary algorithms. Contrary to traditional methods, which prioritize uniformity in parallelization, the algorithm takes into consideration the inherent bias towards evaluation time differences and adjusts accordingly. By measuring the gap between early and late evaluations, the algorithm decides which function values to complete first, thus reducing the bias-induced delay. The benefits of this innovative method are verified through comprehensive analysis and diverse case studies involving varying levels of parallelism and convergence performance.

The planetary system surrounding HD 80979, initially identified by a direct imaging team in 2012, comprises a planet with a relatively large mass orbiting a star near the boundary where stellar systems transition to sub-brown dwarf systems, a point of interest for the power law that describes mass ratios. Our study utilizes radial velocity data to refine HD 80979's basic characteristics, including its mass, which is now known to be near 0.8 solar masses and slightly smaller than its original size. By combining this data with the results of a study on microlensing, we were able to determine the mass of the planet accurately, which is now known to be near 25 Jupiter masses, marking the boundary where stars transition to sub-brown dwarf systems. Our study reveals a system with a planet with a mass near that of brown dwarfs orbiting a star with a relatively small mass difference between them.

The concept of an effective, time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian underpins the Floquet engineering of quasi-static systems through high-frequency driving. However, existing research has not yet fully explored the quantum engineering of non-equilibrium systems. Our analysis reveals that the effective Floquet generator comprises two distinct phases characterized by Gaussian and Borel-Riesz behaviors. We demonstrate the application of the Floquet engineering approach to static and dynamic quantum state preparations, specifically utilizing Gaussian states and squeezed vacua, to achieve their desired effects.

Our research examined the structural, magnetic, and electronic characteristics of CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_{x}$ for $x$ ranging from $0.2$ to $0.8$. Our findings based on magnetization measurements, neutron diffraction, and the calculation of the density of states revealed that non-ordered magnetic phases were identified solely in samples containing $x$ greater than approximately $0.6$. These results revealed a transition from antiferromagnetic interactions at lower $x$ values to ferromagnetic interactions at higher $x$ values, resulting in magnetic properties that were heavily influenced by quantum mechanical mixing.

Using the 150-m radio telescope in Badari, we conducted observations of neutral hydrogen in three regions of high mass star formation near the Galactic center. We observed strong signals of self-absorption in the HI spectrum at velocities close to the local standard of rest, and further analysis revealed that these signals are linked to cold and dense molecular gas near the Galactic center. Our calculations indicate the presence of molecular gas with a mass of approximately 0.01 to 0.03 solar masses, consistent with values of both gas and stars in the area. We detected significant variations in velocity and total pressure between different spectral lines and found it necessary to consider both thermal pressure caused by hot gas and turbulence in the region. Our observations suggest self-gravitation caused by high mass star formation may be responsible for the observed self-absorption, and our findings demonstrate the ability to detect these phenomena even at high temperatures.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, which yields the first comprehensive study of the dynamical properties of such transformations, including an in-depth analysis of the measure-theoretic behavior of these transformations, which proves to be self-affine, obtained as a direct consequence of the self-similar nature of the images of the maps in the corresponding symbolic dynamics.

The study of rare $B$ decays in a high-energy collider environment has become a crucial source of potential new physics. Focusing on $B^{\pm}$ decays to specific final states, we've carried out an in-depth analysis using a dataset of integrated luminosity of 1.04 fb$^{-1}$ collected from $e^+e^-$ collisions at the BEPCII and the TFEEC detectors, which was taken during 2016-2018. With this data, we've confirmed the occurrence of the $B^{\pm}\to K^{\pm}K^+K^-$ process, yielding a significant measurement, and we've derived precise branching ratios for $B^{\pm}\to K^{\mp}K^+K^-$, yielding $(2.73\pm 0.32 \pm 0.14)\times 10^{-6}$, and for $B^{\pm}\to K^{\mp}\pi^+K^-$, yielding $(2.17\pm 0.19 \pm 0.10)\times 10^{-6}$.

It's widely acknowledged that deep neural networks excel at extracting key features from data, but they often falter when facing tasks involving datasets with distinct underlying patterns. Current techniques to enhance generalization typically rely on transferring knowledge from related datasets. We propose an alternative approach to improve representation learning from a single dataset by leveraging unsupervised knowledge transfer. Our method, TAPIR, employs two interconnected networks, each tasked with specific objectives: one to minimize reconstruction losses, the other to maximize alignment with target style features while preserving semantic integrity through association with the primary network. We assess the effectiveness of TAPIR on image classification, stylistic transformation, and semantic segmentation tasks, and observe notable improvements in its ability to make accurate predictions.

In a two-dimensional space of a finite field, any line does not pass through all the points, and by definition, a set of at least three points, where no proper subset lies on a single line, constitutes an arc in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$. This study provides the complete list of all arcs present in the plane of the field $\mathbb{F}_q^2$, for the specific values of $q$ and through a method such as using a three-dimensional space of the field $\mathbb{F}_q$.

A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between four-point equilateral triangles and all possible equilateral triangles. This reveals that both have the same number of configurations. Furthermore, a new formula is derived for counting the number of equilateral triangles with height equal to $kn$, where $1\le k<n$.

Artificial Intelligence applications heavily rely on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), but their operational mechanisms remain unclear, making it challenging to assess their reliability, biases, and accuracy. In an effort to address this, researchers have developed post-hoc explanation methods, however, these methods primarily involve aggregating data and often require significant computational resources. As a result, they can be slow and, in some cases, inaccurate by explaining simplified versions of the original post-hoc methods. To address these issues, we have created FastGraph, a new global post-hoc explanation method for non-linear GNNs that balances speed and accuracy. FastGraph employs a two-stage process, where it initially identifies key areas and then uses that information to build a more precise model. In our experiments, FastGraph demonstrated significant improvements, achieving up to 50x faster explanation generation and more accurate results compared to existing state-of-the-art post-hoc methods for GNNs, while also providing more efficient use of computational resources and faster training times.

The system RXCJ0232.2-4420 is the second in a series of recently identified Chandra sources within the 2XMM-XXC sample that exhibit a core/shell structure. An examination of this group reveals that 2XMM-XXC system 0232.2-4420 is the only one to possess a cool core. KappaMap analysis of XMM-Newton data indicates the presence of heat flux along the system's shell, pointing towards the potential of RXCJ0232.2-4420 being the result of ongoing or past mergers. Examination of XMM-Newton and XMM-Newton/MOS data shows that the low-mass X-ray emitting gas is rotating at 100-200 km/s, while the high-mass X-ray emitting gas has a higher velocity, suggesting that the rotating system is composed of multiple components. XMM-Newton/MOS data also shows that the low-mass X-ray emitting gas has a higher velocity dispersion, suggesting that it has been involved in a merger event. Optical and HST imaging reveals the presence of two potential groups of galaxies, separated by 200-300 kpc, and further investigation of galaxy positions within the XMM-Newton/MOS data shows that the lower mass component contains more galaxies, suggesting that it may be the product of multiple merger events.

A new type of recurrent neural network, based on kernel methods, is introduced and called the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU). Leveraging orthogonal polynomials and exploiting parallel processing capabilities, the LMU achieves significant matrix operations without the need for traditional recurrent connections. Evaluation results using various benchmark datasets and tasks confirm that LMU units can replace Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units while also outperforming transformer-based models that employ self-attention mechanisms. Notably, LMU units feature simpler architecture and reduced parameter requirements compared to existing architectures.

In recent years, there's been heightened interest in feebly interacting particles like dark matter particles and the long-sought lepton flavor violating decay of the Z boson. This interest stems from their potential to offer new insights into fundamental physics and engineering principles. Developing sensitive detectors capable of observing rare events is crucial for both areas. This paper introduces the concept of functional feedback loops for particle physics research, allowing experts to provide input on particle types, experimental environments, and detection methods, thereby informing researchers on how to design experiments. It's then applied to identify relevant detectors like particle trackers, time projections chambers, and dual-phase time projection chambers, suggesting areas of improvement, and ultimately, informing particle physics research on future detector developments.

Language evolution has been the subject of multiple theoretical models in recent years, often grounded in various areas of research, and the analysis of language dynamics as a form of complex public phenomenon has become a key component of this research, falling under the broader field of public sociology. Public sociology seeks to understand and model language changes as they occur within a given population, focusing on the shifts in language behavior as a result of individual and collective actions. This study specifically examines how human migration affects language changes, modeling language changes as a form of resource competition, with an individual's language being seen as a resource that can be acquired, lost, or shared, depending on their interactions with others. Through exploring various migration patterns, we demonstrate the impact of different migration types on the language changes that occur, revealing the complex relationship between migration and language changes as a form of resource competition.

PINN methods have shown significant potential in solving various complex mathematical problems. However, they often encounter difficulties in handling PDEs with high-frequency features, leading to inconsistent convergence despite increasing neural network width. To address this, we have developed a novel deep learning method for PDE initial value problems by introducing a multi-scale neural network in frequency space. By utilizing the Fast Fourier Transform, we can isolate and solve high-frequency components, while focusing the main network on the smoother solution. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, particularly in generating the smooth solution component and achieving high accuracy, even for problems with intricate high-frequency features. Furthermore, we have successfully applied this method to various mathematical problems and observed high accuracy, while also enabling PINN convergence by increasing the network's width.

We examine a two-wave system in a bounded domain that undergoes partial Kelvin-Voigt damping on one wave and cubic damping on the other wave. We demonstrate the exponential decay of energy affecting the wavedampened by viscosity and the algebraic decay of energy, with a rate of one over the time raised to the power of three-fifths, affecting the wavedampened by the cubic damping.

To tackle system optimization, deep reinforcement learning has become a leading approach, despite its own set of challenges, namely sample inefficiency and lack of theoretical transparency. This paper draws on a historical method of optimization and develops two new techniques to address these challenges, thereby enabling more effective policy learning and providing more reliable results. To address sample inefficiency, we developed an innovative method that combines existing models with data-driven approaches to utilize unobserved information more effectively. This hybrid approach significantly improves the efficiency of policy learning and its real-world effectiveness across different visual recognition tasks and control problems. To address the need for theoretical clarity, we developed new theoretical frameworks to address adversarial training issues, thereby providing more reliable methods for robust policy learning and providing clear guidelines and quantifiable metrics. To facilitate open-source research and improve task-specific performance, we developed a suite of tailored network architectures and training strategies, supported by source code, narrative guides, and pre-trained models. This comprehensive framework has been successfully applied to diverse data formats and different control problems, yielding significant and reliable performance improvements over existing state-of-the-art approaches across different control problems, computer vision tasks, and graph-based problems.

We've developed a comprehensive theory for achieving optical nonreciprocity in a shared cavity's individual modes, a concept first demonstrated in 2021 by (arXiv:2104.07744). Unlike previous approaches, this mechanism relies on quantum squeezing rather than classical waves or quantum squeezing of the shared cavity's collective modes. Our findings show that any cavity with two or more modes can exhibit nonreciprocity when coupled to a single qubit driven by an off-resonant microwave signal. This mechanism relies on an effective nonlinearity generated by qubit-mediated interactions between specific pairs of the shared cavity's modes. Using both analytical and numerical methods, we calculated the conditions necessary for achieving significant quantum squeezing-induced optical nonreciprocity. These conditions were experimentally feasible within the parameters of the experiment conducted in (Nature 2021).

We demonstrate that for a set of concave kernel functions including the cosine similarity, inner product, and kernel sigmoid, optimizing certain kernel-based tasks under a bounded norm constraint results in an infinite number of solutions accumulating at the boundary of that constraint. Consequently, these tasks exhibit no global optimum. Furthermore, we show that under certain bounded norm constraints, the objective function's derivatives become unbounded, rendering these tasks incompatible with gradient-based optimization methods. Interestingly, contrary to expectations, these tasks aren't conducive to emerging regularization techniques, specifically for a particular kernel, they lack a local optimum outside of the bounded norm constraint's boundary. However, by merging the bounded norm constraint with additional regularization, we obtain related tasks, including regularized versions of logistic regression and auto-encoding, and prove these tasks admit a global optimum that can be efficiently computed using established optimization methods, including gradient descent, due to their convex objectives.

The CRESST experiment, which employs calcium carbonate crystals, is capable of thoroughly exploring a wide range of dark matter particles. A novel feature of the experiment is its ability to carry out the search across various running parameters. The latest CRESST-II results are presented here, encompassing the superlight domain up to 0.5 eV. The focus of this report is on the methods, particularly those involving the adjustment of the investigation range, the data analysis, and the considerations for background events. The focus here is on CRESST-II's performance within the non-resonant operation mode.

Blind image deblurring is a challenging inverse problem, and the blurring process is a linear transformation that can be represented by a linear combination of kernels with unknown weights. This study introduces an efficient linear-time image deblurring method based on a novel kernel mixture model that leverages efficient algorithms to calculate the kernel mixture. The KEMIX model outperforms existing methods in terms of both performance and efficiency, with comparison results showing superior image quality and faster processing times compared to state-of-the-art deblurring algorithms.

This paper introduces a new concept, namely associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with a double curvature, which serves as a generalized, double curvature-dependent counterpart to the Rota-Baxter system's bijective pair. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Rota-Baxter system with double curvature is intrinsically linked to the BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with a double curvature, and the Rota-Baxter system with double curvature is also intrinsically linked to the BiHom-Yang-Baxter system with a double curvature. Ultimately, using the BiHom-Yang-Baxter system and the BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with various levels of symmetry, new BiHom-commutative algebras can be constructed.

Formal verification methods, like those employing static analysis, can assist developers in creating reliable software by automatically detecting potential errors before it's released. Hoare logic offers a precise way to describe desired program behavior, but it requires manual identification of relevant invariants, a task that can be challenging for developers to accomplish consistently. Despite advancements in using neural networks to assist in formal verification, current methods struggle to leverage the full potential of available domain knowledge due to difficulties in representing domain-specific information in neural network layers. Our solution involves a neural network-based program analyzer called DeepVerify, which integrates analytical information from static analysis in embedding vectors to inform invariant identification within the context of target programs. Furthermore, we define a new metric to quantify the impact of integration methods on analysis accuracy, demonstrating that, on average, this approach reduces error rates by 20% compared to existing methods. Additionally, we propose a method that automatically generates domain knowledge by converting code, and experimental results show that this increases analysis accuracy by 15%.

A distributed consensus protocol is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The concept behind it is straightforward, involving the process of different nodes reaching agreement on a particular state or data, in spite of the presence of faulty nodes. However, achieving this agreement poses significant challenges, primarily due to the high latency and the need to minimize the communication required, especially with the constant need to exchange data as part of the process, which can be costly. To overcome these challenges, this research introduces Canopus, a novel distributed consensus protocol that leverages asynchronous channels and optimizes communication by only exchanging messages when necessary, which is determined by local computations. By utilizing data locality, the protocol reduces the communication load and improves overall performance. To evaluate the benefits of Canopus, it has been compared against well-known approaches such as PBFT, Raft, and Paxos, resulting in up to a 10-fold performance improvement.

The phase behavior of cholesterol within lipid bilayers significantly impacts its interaction with embedded proteins. Cholesterol's concentration in the bilayer affects its mechanical properties, thereby influencing how it deforms around membrane proteins. By utilizing a continuum model, which treats the lipid bilayer as a two-dimensional fluid, and applying linear elasticity theory, the work focuses on understanding the optimal path of membrane deformation required for the cholesterol concentration profile to minimize energy costs under certain assumptions. By applying the derived principles to a model membrane containing a protein with a specific bending modulus and cholesterol concentration, the work investigates how the optimization equation behaves. By applying the optimization principles to a membrane containing a single protein with a specific size and characteristics, the work identifies two distinct regimes in which the optimization equation has distinct solutions and in each regime, the work examines how the optimization equation behaves and how it compares to experimental findings. By extending the analysis to membranes containing multiple proteins, the work investigates how the optimization equation can be applied to understand the effects of protein interactions on membrane behavior.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. It looks at a spatially homogeneous, flat FRW model and finds that its quantum behavior differs significantly from its classical counterpart. Unlike its classical version, the model possesses a unique state that cannot be achieved from its state of infinite curvature, making it impossible for the universe to expand beyond a certain point. Additionally, the article explores the implications of this model on the universe's future, revealing a period of accelerated expansion, followed by a potential big bounce, and finally a gradual deceleration, all of which differs from the predictions made by classical cosmology.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a range 
from 30 to 240 EeV (equivalent to 30-240 exa-electronvolts). Each event in 
this dataset is accompanied by precise time and location information, allowing 
for an exact reconstruction of the primary particle's direction, as well as an 
estimated energy level with a precision of one decade. This collection enables 
an in-depth examination of the cosmic rays that triggered the Auger Observatory.

Deep neural networks have become a popular approach to complex robotic systems due to their remarkable learning capabilities. Nonetheless, processing continuous, real-world data like sensor data remains a problem for deep neural networks, which typically require discrete data inputs. This paper examines the limitations of applying category-based loss functions to uncertain, continuous data in robotic systems. Specifically, we focus on the challenge of making precise position predictions to control robotic arms. Our study demonstrates that predicting target values is suboptimal, but uncertainty quantification is crucial. Based on this insight, we propose a novel uncertainty quantification method that generates category-based uncertainty estimates for real-valued predictions, which is suitable for robotic systems. Our uncertainty quantification approach is first evaluated through simulations and then tested on a robotic arm system, which achieves superior results compared to existing techniques, according to our experiments.

The traffic forecasting task is crucial for developing effective transportation systems.
Current traffic forecasting models rely heavily on reducing the spatial dimension
by aggregating sensor readings, which limits their ability to capture the traffic
conditions at the patch level. This research proposes a novel approach,
STL-2-CNN, which effectively analyzes traffic time series at a granular level and
CNNs are applied independently to each small region to improve CNN performance and
allow it to adapt to local traffic patterns. The CNN can also replace the previous
CNN+LSTM method and achieve better results. The experimental results demonstrate the
benefit of dividing test data into smaller tiles to increase STL-2-CNN's prediction
accuracy and robustness. The CNN-LSTM approach outperforms the previous
methods, demonstrating the importance of considering both temporal and spatial
factors in the traffic forecasting problem.

In recent years, RE-morphisms have been used to study the structure of pseudomonoidal and strict Gray categories. This research demonstrates that RE-morphisms on Gray categories comprise the widest possible category of tricategories. Moreover, it is shown that any Gray category modification can be achieved through a sequence of modifications at the level of 2-morphisms. Finally, re-morphisms on Gray categories can be seen as the widest possible tricategory expansions.

Hippocampus segmentation is crucial in diagnosing various neuropsychiatric conditions, such as Alzheimer's disease, and its research is highly relevant in these fields. Despite advancements, existing methods are limited, especially in the manual segmentation of the hippocampus, which is time-consuming, and automated approaches are still underdeveloped. We have developed an innovative deep learning framework, called Dense-Space-Scale Fusion Network (D-SSFN), which effectively segment the hippocampus by merging multi-scale features from both a dense encoder and multiple decoders. The Dense encoder integrates a deep space convolutional block along with a spatial attention mechanism, while several Scale decoders combine low-frequency features with high-resolution features to capture essential low-level details. The D-SSFN framework outperformed other top methods in multiple evaluation metrics, demonstrating its ability to accurately segment the hippocampus. Our study's unique contributions lie in its exploration of low-frequency details through multiple decoders, the exploration of a dense encoder with a space convolutional block, and the integration of a space attention mechanism. Our code is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ghk199/D-SSFN.

Our research indicates a significant presence of protons in Earth's inner radiation belt that originate from cosmic ray antiprotons colliding with the space around us. To understand why this does not lead to an even greater concentration of protons, we have developed a comprehensive mathematical model of the process, which is suitable for comparison with actual data.
